input:
When a liquid mixture behaves ideally, Raoult's law provides a simple and remarkably powerful way to estimate the partial pressure exerted by each component in the vapour above the mixture. In the present example, the mixture consists of hexane dissolved in heptane, and the focus is on the more volatile component, whose mole fraction in the liquid phase, denoted by $x$, is 0.23. At the temperature of the mixture, the pure-component vapour pressure of this component, denoted by $P^*$, is 12.7 kPa. Raoult's law relates these quantities through the following expression:

$$p = x P^*$$

In other words, the partial pressure $p$ is obtained simply by multiplying the liquid mole fraction by the pure-component vapour pressure, which in this case gives a value of 2.9 kPa. It is important to note that this relationship rests on the assumption of an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules are essentially the same as those between like molecules. Because hexane and heptane are chemically very similar, this assumption is often considered reasonable, although it remains an idealisation. Furthermore, no activity coefficients are applied for the real mixture, meaning that any deviations from ideal behaviour are not captured by this estimate. Overall, the calculation illustrates how a single, elegant relationship can deliver a useful first estimate of a partial pressure from nothing more than a composition and a pure-component vapour pressure, underscoring the enduring value of Raoult's law in mixture thermodynamics. It is also worth emphasising that the result is tied to the temperature at which the pure-component vapour pressure is quoted, since vapour pressures are strongly temperature-dependent quantities; a different temperature would produce a different pure-component value and hence a different partial pressure, even at exactly the same liquid composition. As such, the estimate should always be read together with the temperature and the composition at which it was obtained.
target:
Raoult's law gives the partial pressure of a component over an ideal liquid mixture as the product of its liquid mole fraction and its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature:

$$p = x P^*$$

Here $p$ is the partial pressure of the volatile component, $x$ is its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ is its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. For hexane in heptane, $x$ is 0.23 and $P^*$ is 12.7 kPa; substitution gives $p$ = 2.9 kPa. Raoult's law holds for an ideal solution, in which interactions between unlike molecules equal those between like molecules. Hexane and heptane are close in structure, and the ideal-solution treatment is the usual first estimate for such a pair. The partial pressure is the component's contribution to the total vapour pressure over the liquid; the second component contributes by the same relation, with its own mole fraction and pure-component vapour pressure. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied, and the estimate carries no correction for departure from ideal-solution behaviour. A mixture that departs from ideality gives a partial pressure off the Raoult value, in the direction and size set by the activity coefficient of the component in the mixture. The estimate is stated at the mixture temperature because the pure-component vapour pressure is a function of temperature: a value of $P^*$ taken at another temperature would give a different partial pressure for the same composition, and the composition itself may shift with temperature where the liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour. The relation is linear in the composition, so the partial pressure tracks the mole fraction directly across the whole composition range of the liquid. At the ends of that range the relation returns the checks its form requires: a liquid of the pure volatile component exerts the pure-component vapour pressure, and a component present in vanishing amount exerts a vanishing partial pressure. No measurement enters the estimate beyond the stated inputs.
